title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, IaC & CI/CD Playbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview:

This playbook consolidates our infrastructure engineering guidance for the GPU serving fleet and adjacent systems: capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/ IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and operational runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate Redwood Inference’s inference clusters (hosted, dedicated, and private variants).

Goals:
- Provide clear ownership and procedures for capacity changes, incident response, and upgrades.
- Standardize Terraform modules and IaC patterns used across GPU nodepools, autoscaling, and networking.
- Define CI/CD practices for safe build, test, and rollout of infra changes.
- Give concrete runbooks and alerts for common failure modes.

Scope:
This doc covers: GPU cluster provisioning (cloud-managed and on-prem), nodepool sizing and autoscaling, cross-account VPC connectivity patterns, Terraform module conventions, CI/CD pipelines for infra repos, key runbooks (capacity, node health, network interruptions), and templates for capacity requests. It does not cover model-serving runtime architecture detail (see eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture).

Ownership and contacts:
- Infra Fleet Team (primary owner): infra-fleet@redwood.example.com
- Cloud Networking (secondary): cloud-networking@redwood.example.com
- Oncall escalation: platform-oncall (PagerDuty)
- SLO owners: SLO-Ownership spreadsheet (linked in related pages)

SLOs, targets, and alerting thresholds:
- Fleet availability (control plane + scheduler): 99.95% monthly uptime target for hosted inference clusters.
- GPU node readiness: target > 98% of provisioned GPUs in Ready state during business hours (PST).
- Pod GPU allocation success rate: >= 99.5% for scheduled inference jobs.
- Scale-up latency for reactive autoscaling: median < 90s; p95 < 240s.
- Cost efficiency: maintain average GPU utilization 60-80% for general-purpose pools; > 40% for reserve/burst pools.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- nodepool-unready: fired when >5% nodes in a nodepool are NotReady for >5 minutes.
- gpu-scheduling-failure-rate: >1% pod scheduling failures due to insufficient GPUs over 10 minutes.
- autoscaler-throttled: external autoscaler reports >3 consecutive failed scale events.

GPU Fleet Architecture (high level):
- Control plane: gpu-scheduler service (k8s-style control loop running on control-plane instances), autoscaler service (nodepool-autoscaler), and provisioning agent (cloud-provisioner).
- Nodepools: logical grouping by instance-type and workload (e.g., p4d-general, a100-highmem, t4-inference). Each nodepool has an associated Terraform module, autoscaling policy, and cost center tag.
- Caching & workload routing: prefix cache nodes run in dedicated pools; latency-sensitive pools are provisioned in local regions.
- Networking: per-account VPCs with peering or Transit Gateway connectivity for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Cloud accounts & networking patterns:
- Account layout: dedicated cloud account per environment (prod-hosted, prod-dedicated, staging, onprem). Use named IAM roles for cross-account access.
- VPC layout: one VPC per account with segmented subnets: control-plane, compute-gpu, mgmt, and egress.
- Networking security: enforce NACLs and security groups; control-plane only accepts traffic from mgmt and internal infra ranges.
- Cross-account routing: prefer Transit Gateway for high-throughput inter-region traffic; use VPC Peering for low-latency single-region links.
- IP allocation: reserve a /20 for GPU compute in each region to avoid exhaustion.

Terraform / IaC modules & conventions:
- Module style: all GPU-related infra uses the shared "gpu-nodepool" module pattern (modules/gpu-nodepool). Each module must expose: nodepool_name, instance_type, gpu_count_per_node, min_size, max_size, labels (map), taints (list), autoscaling_policy (object as JSON string).
- Tagging and cost allocation: every resource must include tags: team, cost_center, environment, project.
- State management: use remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking (prod accounts). State file naming convention: terraform-state/<account>/<region>/<component>.tfstate.
- Module publishing: modules live in git under infra/modules. Releases are created by CI with semver tags and CHANGELOG enforcement.

Recommended Terraform snippets (example inlined):

module "gpu_nodepool_p4d" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu-nodepool?ref=v1.3.0"
  nodepool_name = "p4d-general"
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  gpu_count_per_node = 8
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 32
  labels = { workload = "inference", tier = "latency-sensitive" }
}

CI/CD and build pipelines (pattern):
- Repo layout: infra/ (component per top-level area), modules/, platform-automation/ (scripts and pipelines).
- Merge criteria: PRs require passing static checks (tflint, terraform fmt), unit test plan (terraform plan in PR), and 2 approvers for prod-targeting changes.
- Branching model: trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches. Releases for modules use tags; infra repo uses gated promotion to staging then prod.
- Pipeline stages (recommended):
  1) Lint & fmt checks
  2) Static analysis (tflint, checkov)
  3) Terraform validate + plan (in ephemeral workspace)
  4) Plan review & approvals (manual for prod)
  5) Apply in controlled runner (applied by platform automation account)
- Security gating: all changes that modify IAM or network must trigger a security review job.

CI example (GitHub Actions simplified):
- .github/workflows/terraform-plan.yml runs on pull_request, produces a plan file and comments the PR with plan summary. Apply workflow runs on push to main with required reviewers.

Runbooks & operational playbooks (select):
1) Capacity shortfall (high-priority):
  - Trigger: gpu-scheduling-failure-rate alert OR sustained GPU utilization > 90% for 30m.
  - Steps:
    1. PagerDuty page to platform-oncall.
    2. Triage: run `kubectl get nodes -l nodepool=<impacted>` and check node statuses.
    3. If autoscaler failing, check autoscaler logs in cloudwatch/stackdriver and restart deployment.
    4. If capacity needed immediately, temporarily increase nodepool max_size (Terraform emergency patch) or launch emergency nodegroup using the provisioning CLI: `infractl nodepool scale --name p4d-general --max 64`.
    5. After stabilization, open post-action ticket and revert emergency changes to original IaC.
2) Node GPU hardware errors:
  - Trigger: kernel or NVML errors reported, GPU ECC errors > threshold.
  - Steps: cordon node, drain pods, run hardware diagnostics, open support case with cloud provider, replace node.
3) Network partition between control-plane & compute:
  - Trigger: control-plane->compute heartbeat missing, multiple nodepools NotReady simultaneously.
  - Steps: verify route tables, Transit Gateway status, VPC flow logs for drop patterns, escalate to cloud-networking.

Upgrade and rollback playbook:
- Canary first: stage changes to a single low-traffic nodepool (canary), observe metrics for 30-60 minutes. If stable, promote to 3 additional nodepools, then to full fleet.
- Rollback triggers: increased pod restart rate > 2x baseline, GPU allocation failures > 0.5% p95, or unexplained instance termination.
- Rollback steps: revert Terraform to previous tag, apply to affected accounts, and monitor. Document every rollout in release_notes/infra.

Capacity planning process (quarterly + event-driven):
- Quarterly review: owners submit expected load growth, new product launches, demo days, and model onboarding plans. Use the capacity planning template (attached) to estimate additional GPUs by region and timeline.
- Event-driven: if marketing or sales expects a spike (new customer onboarding, feature launch), create an expedited capacity request and follow the emergency provisioning checklist.

Templates and artifacts (where to find):
- Terraform modules: github.com/redwood/infra-modules (modules/gpu-nodepool)
- CI templates: infra/.github/workflows/
- Capacity request template: docs/templates/gpu-capacity-request.md (links in related pages)
- Diagnostics scripts: infra/tools/gpu-diagnostics.sh

Operational notes and best practices:
- Prefer homogenous nodepools per workload class to simplify scheduling and binpacking.
- Use spot/interruptible instances for non-latency critical workloads; ensure eviction policies are in place.
- Enforce IAM least privilege for provisioning roles.
- Keep Terraform plans small and focused; multi-component applies should be gated and coordinated with owners.

Post-incident actions and triage:
- Every Sev2+ incident requires a postmortem with timeline, contributing factors, remediation, and action owners. Postmortem must be created within 72 hours and assigned to the incident commander.

Appendix: quick CLI commands and checks:
- Check nodepool health: `kubectl get nodes -l nodepool=<name> -o wide`
- View autoscaler status: `kubectl -n infra logs deploy/nodepool-autoscaler`
- Terraform plan in ephemeral workspace: `terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan`
- Emergency scale (CLI): `infractl nodepool scale --name <name> --max <count>`

Notes and references:
- Related runbooks and detailed guides are linked at the top of the page. For private/onprem packaging and upgrade guides see eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures.
